question: What does an anti-harassment policy actually have to contain, and how much of that is required?
aliases: minimum contents of a harassment policy
are EEOC promising practices legally required
what should a harassment complaint procedure say
shortAnswer: Less is currently in force than most checklists assume, so start with what each document is. The EEOC's 1999 enforcement guidance on vicarious liability states that an anti-harassment policy and complaint procedure should contain, at a minimum, a clear explanation of prohibited conduct [S:eeoc-guidance-vicarious-liability-supervisor-harassment], but that document was replaced on April 29, 2024 [S:eeoc-enforcement-guidance-harassment-workplace-2024], and its replacement was itself partly vacated in May 2025 and then rescinded by Commission vote on January 22, 2026 [S:eeoc-enforcement-guidance-harassment-workplace-2024][S:eeoc-newsroom-rescind-2024-harassment-guidance]. The Promising Practices document remains published and says of itself that it is not a strict legal requirement under federal law [S:eeoc-promising-practices-preventing-harassment].
assumes: You are asking what these federal documents say a policy should contain, and are willing to read their current status alongside their contents. A state may impose its own requirements, and this record does not describe any state's.
You are asking what the documents say, not what legal effect a compliant policy has. None of the records consulted here states that effect.
You accept that a rescinded or superseded document still tells you what the agency once considered adequate, which is useful, while not being current enforcement guidance.
why:
Before the lists, the status, because it changes what they are. The 1999 enforcement guidance carries a notice on its own page that it was superseded on April 29, 2024 [S:eeoc-guidance-vicarious-liability-supervisor-harassment], by a document the Commission approved that day on a 3-2 vote, which replaced it and several other earlier guidance documents [S:eeoc-enforcement-guidance-harassment-workplace-2024]. On May 15, 2025 a federal court in Texas, et al. v. EEOC declared unlawful and vacated portions of that replacement, stating that the vacatur of the unlawful portions applies nationwide [S:eeoc-enforcement-guidance-harassment-workplace-2024]. The Commission then voted 2-1 on January 22, 2026 to rescind it, announced the following day, and the announcement names no document issued in its place [S:eeoc-newsroom-rescind-2024-harassment-guidance]. The Chair stated that the federal laws against discrimination, harassment and retaliation, and the Supreme Court precedent interpreting them, remain firmly in place [S:eeoc-newsroom-rescind-2024-harassment-guidance].

So what follows describes what the agency has published rather than what it currently enforces. That is still worth reading: it is the most detailed public account of what the EEOC has treated as adequate, and the statutes it was written about did not move. It is not a checklist anyone can hold up as current federal guidance.
Take the minimum list first, because it is short and it was stated as a minimum. The 1999 guidance says an anti-harassment policy and complaint procedure should contain, at a minimum, a clear explanation of prohibited conduct [S:eeoc-guidance-vicarious-liability-supervisor-harassment]. Alongside it the same guidance lists: assurance that employees who complain or provide information related to complaints will be protected against retaliation [S:eeoc-guidance-vicarious-liability-supervisor-harassment]; a clearly described complaint process providing accessible avenues of complaint [S:eeoc-guidance-vicarious-liability-supervisor-harassment]; assurance that the employer will protect the confidentiality of complaints to the extent possible [S:eeoc-guidance-vicarious-liability-supervisor-harassment]; a complaint process providing a prompt, thorough and impartial investigation [S:eeoc-guidance-vicarious-liability-supervisor-harassment]; and assurance that the employer will take immediate and appropriate corrective action when it determines harassment has occurred [S:eeoc-guidance-vicarious-liability-supervisor-harassment].

Six elements. Notice that four of the six are promises the policy makes rather than rules it imposes: protection against retaliation, confidentiality, a proper investigation, and corrective action. A policy that only prohibits conduct has one of the six.

The guidance is equally specific about getting it in front of people. An employer should provide every employee with a copy of the policy and complaint procedure, and redistribute it periodically [S:eeoc-guidance-vicarious-liability-supervisor-harassment]. Other means of dissemination include posting the policy in central locations and incorporating it into employee handbooks [S:eeoc-guidance-vicarious-liability-supervisor-harassment]. And on training: if feasible, the employer should provide training to all employees to ensure they understand their rights and responsibilities [S:eeoc-guidance-vicarious-liability-supervisor-harassment], with supervisors receiving periodic training covering prohibited conduct, the seriousness of the policy, supervisor responsibilities on learning of harassment, and the prohibition on retaliation [S:eeoc-guidance-vicarious-liability-supervisor-harassment].

The Promising Practices document then fills in what each element looks like when it is done well. The description of prohibited conduct should be easy to understand and include examples [S:eeoc-promising-practices-preventing-harassment]. The retaliation statement should be unequivocal and should name the protected activities: reporting harassing conduct, participating in investigations, or taking any other action protected under federal employment discrimination laws [S:eeoc-promising-practices-preventing-harassment]. The complaint system description should name multiple, easily accessible reporting avenues where possible [S:eeoc-promising-practices-preventing-harassment]. The investigation promise should be prompt, impartial and thorough [S:eeoc-promising-practices-preventing-harassment]. The confidentiality promise should say whose identity is protected, naming those who report, alleged victims, witnesses and alleged harassers, to the extent possible and permitted by law and consistent with a thorough and impartial investigation [S:eeoc-promising-practices-preventing-harassment]. And the corrective action assurance should be of immediate and proportionate action [S:eeoc-promising-practices-preventing-harassment].

One word there is worth pausing on. The enforcement guidance says appropriate corrective action [S:eeoc-guidance-vicarious-liability-supervisor-harassment]; the Promising Practices document says proportionate [S:eeoc-promising-practices-preventing-harassment]. They are not the same word and a policy has to pick one.

On form and delivery, the Promising Practices document asks that a policy be comprehensive, easy to understand, and regularly communicated to all employees [S:eeoc-promising-practices-preventing-harassment], written and communicated in a clear, easy to understand style and format [S:eeoc-promising-practices-preventing-harassment], and provided to employees upon hire and during harassment trainings as well as posted centrally, such as on an internal website, in the handbook, near time clocks, in break rooms and in other commonly used locations [S:eeoc-promising-practices-preventing-harassment].

Now the weight question, which the EEOC answers about its own document rather than leaving to inference. The Promising Practices are described as promising practices rather than strict legal requirements under federal law [S:eeoc-promising-practices-preventing-harassment], and the document says that although these practices are not legal requirements under federal employment discrimination laws, they may enhance employers' compliance efforts [S:eeoc-promising-practices-preventing-harassment]. So the detailed version is guidance about doing it well, not a statute. The shorter list sits in enforcement guidance on vicarious liability for supervisor harassment and is framed as a minimum [S:eeoc-guidance-vicarious-liability-supervisor-harassment].

What neither document does, in the material recorded here, is state what legal consequence follows from having or lacking any of it. That is a question for a lawyer and it is not answered on this page.
whatChanges: Whether the policy carries all six elements of the minimum list or only prohibits conduct [S:eeoc-guidance-vicarious-liability-supervisor-harassment].
Whether the retaliation statement names the protected activities or merely mentions retaliation [S:eeoc-promising-practices-preventing-harassment].
Whether the confidentiality promise says whose identity is protected, including witnesses and alleged harassers [S:eeoc-promising-practices-preventing-harassment].

Whether corrective action is promised as appropriate or as proportionate, since the two documents use different words [S:eeoc-guidance-vicarious-liability-supervisor-harassment][S:eeoc-promising-practices-preventing-harassment].
Whether the policy was actually given to every employee and redistributed periodically, rather than existing [S:eeoc-guidance-vicarious-liability-supervisor-harassment].
Whether supervisors receive periodic training covering their own responsibilities on learning of harassment [S:eeoc-guidance-vicarious-liability-supervisor-harassment].
Which of the two documents you are being measured against, since one is enforcement guidance and the other says it is not a legal requirement [S:eeoc-promising-practices-preventing-harassment].
variability: The EEOC states of its Promising Practices that they are not legal requirements under federal employment discrimination laws, though they may enhance compliance efforts [S:eeoc-promising-practices-preventing-harassment]. Treating them as a statutory checklist overstates them.

The sources consulted here describe what a policy should contain and how it should be distributed. They do not state what legal effect a compliant policy has, or what follows from a deficient one, and nothing on this page should be read as stating either.
This is federal guidance. State law may require more, and a state requirement is not described here.

The 1999 guidance is superseded and its replacement is rescinded [S:eeoc-guidance-vicarious-liability-supervisor-harassment][S:eeoc-enforcement-guidance-harassment-workplace-2024][S:eeoc-newsroom-rescind-2024-harassment-guidance]. Promising Practices remains published [S:eeoc-promising-practices-preventing-harassment]. Nothing here states what the EEOC currently enforces, and the rescission announcement names no replacement document [S:eeoc-newsroom-rescind-2024-harassment-guidance].
nextActions: Read your policy against the six-element minimum list and mark which elements are actually present [S:eeoc-guidance-vicarious-liability-supervisor-harassment].
Check that the retaliation clause names participating in an investigation, not only making a complaint [S:eeoc-promising-practices-preventing-harassment].
Establish how the policy reaches new hires, since it is to be provided upon hire and during trainings [S:eeoc-promising-practices-preventing-harassment].
Set a date to redistribute it, because periodic redistribution is part of what the guidance asks [S:eeoc-guidance-vicarious-liability-supervisor-harassment].
Give supervisors separate periodic training on their own duty when they learn of harassment [S:eeoc-guidance-vicarious-liability-supervisor-harassment].
Take the legal effect of any gap to an employment lawyer rather than inferring it from the guidance, which does not state it.
author: Aaron Bollinger

handoff.reason: The sources describe what a policy should contain and say nothing about what legal consequence attaches to a gap. That consequence is the thing an employer actually needs to know, and it is a question for an employment lawyer.

correction.was: The record cited the EEOC 1999 enforcement guidance as current agency guidance and said nothing about its status. That document had carried a supersession notice since April 29, 2024, its replacement was partly vacated in May 2025 and rescinded in January 2026, and this corpus already recorded all three steps in a walkthrough dated 2026-09-01.
correction.now: The status chain is stated before the contents, the record says plainly that it describes what the agency has published rather than what it currently enforces, and the sources establishing supersession and rescission are cited.
